plan.topic: What to eat on tirzepatide (and semaglutide): protein, fibre, fluids and easier meals when appetite drops, based on the 2025 joint nutrition advisory (ACLM/ASN/OMA/TOS) and dietary guidelines
plan.angle: Lane A, 'Life on GLP-1'. Hook (15 s or less) with no news peg: 'When tirzepatide turns your appetite down, what you eat matters more. By the end you'll know what experts recommend for protein, fiber, fluids and easier meals.' First answer: the 2025 joint advisory from four US nutrition and obesity groups recommends building smaller meals around a protein food, adding fiber gradually and drinking fluids through the day. Chapters as planned. Every habit is 'recommended by the advisory/guidelines', never 'proven on tirzepatide'. Include the kidney-disease protein caveat, the fluid-restriction caveat, 'start strength training gently', the GI side effects, 'don't change your medicines on your own', and the full prescriber line, plus 'consider asking for a registered dietitian referral'.
plan.working_title: What to Eat on Tirzepatide (Mounjaro): Protein, Fibre, Meals
plan.why: Playbook Lane A title with top practical search demand from new starters and a timely Oct 20 hook. It rests on settled guideline evidence, so it can pass the fact-check, and it doesn't repeat any Short from the last 14 days. | fact-check: Good Lane A topic: people search for it, it's evergreen and safe if habits stay 'recommended'. One problem: I couldn't find a Conversation nutrition guide for new GLP-1 starters dated Oct 20, 2026. The closest Conversation piece is an older one about raising your own GLP-1 through food ('What and how you eat can increase the effects of GLP-1 without drugs'). That's a different topic and isn't about medicine users. Don't hang the hook on a source we can't confirm. Build the script on the 2025 joint nutrition advisory (ACLM/ASN/OMA/TOS) plus national dietary guidelines and the drug labels (for delayed stomach emptying and GI side effects). Give protein amounts only as the advisory's 'recommended' ranges, and say 'check with your clinician first if you have kidney disease or have been told to limit protein'. Fluids: 'unless you've been told to limit fluids'. Fibre: 'build up gradually'. No calorie targets, no meal-skipping, no 'GLP-1 diet' claims. Mention nausea, constipation and diarrhoea as common, usually mild to moderate. Only name 'How Long Does Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Take to Work?' as watch-next if it is already published with that exact title; otherwise name another published Lane A video or say 'follow for more'. Small title fix: most of our audience is US and searches 'fiber', so use 'What to Eat on Tirzepatide (Mounjaro): Protein, Fiber, Meals' (60 characters or fewer). Log lane A.

package.description: What to eat on tirzepatide (Mounjaro) or semaglutide when appetite drops: a 2025 joint advisory from four US nutrition and obesity groups recommends regular, smaller meals with enough protein, fiber and fluids. The advisory suggests eating protein-rich foods first (kidney disease, or told to limit protein? check with your clinician first). We also cover building fiber up gradually and sipping fluids through the day, unless you've been told to limit fluids. Nausea, diarrhea, vomiting and constipation are among the most common side effects. If vomiting, diarrhea or severe stomach pain won't settle, contact your clinician, and don't change, skip or stop your medicine on your own. General information, not personal medical advice. Tirzepatide and semaglutide are prescription medicines. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you. Sources: Joint nutrition advisory (ACLM, ASN, OMA, TOS), Obesity, 2025: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12304835/ NHS, Water, drinks and your health: https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/eat-well/food-guidelines-and-food-labels/water-drinks-nutrition/ NHS, How to get more fibre into your diet: https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/eat-well/digestive-health/how-to-get-more-fibre-into-your-diet/ NHS, Dehydration: https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/dehydration/

script.working_title: What to Eat on Tirzepatide (Mounjaro): Protein, Fiber, Meals
script.hook_pattern: Visceral 'you' scenario (four bites and you're full) plus an open loop (the plate trick, paid off near the end). Lane A, Life on GLP-1 series.

scenes.narration: It's dinnertime. You made a proper meal, and four bites in, you're done. If you're on tirzepatide or semaglutide, that moment probably feels familiar.

visual.stock_query: surprised person full after few bites at dinner

scenes.narration: When the medicine turns your appetite down, what you eat matters more. By the end, you'll know what experts recommend for protein, fiber, fluids, and easier meals.

visual.stock_query: curious person looking at four food icons

scenes.retention_device: Explicit promise of what viewer will know

scenes.narration: Here's the first answer. A 2025 joint advisory from four US nutrition and obesity groups recommends regular, smaller meals with enough protein, enough fiber, and enough fluids.

visual.stock_query: friendly experts handing over a meal guide

scenes.narration: Those groups are the American College of Lifestyle Medicine, the American Society for Nutrition, the Obesity Medicine Association, and The Obesity Society.

visual.stock_query: four labelled expert badges on a table

scenes.narration: And stay to the end, because I'll share one simple plate trick that helps a small appetite work for you, not against you.

visual.stock_query: mystery plate under a silver cloche

scenes.retention_device: Main open loop planted (paid off in The plate trick)

scenes.narration: Quick note: this is general education, not personal advice. These are prescription medicines, so talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

visual.stock_query: Medi mascot pointing to doctor's office

scenes.narration: Now picture someone we'll call Sam, a hypothetical 54-year-old, three weeks into treatment. Sam's question is simple: if I'm barely hungry, what should actually go on my plate?

visual.stock_query: thoughtful man staring at half-eaten plate

scenes.retention_device: Relatable thread introduced with a question

scenes.narration: First, why does appetite drop so much? After you eat, your gut releases a hormone called GLP-1. It helps signal fullness and helps manage blood sugar.

visual.stock_query: gut sending glowing message to brain

scenes.narration: Semaglutide acts like that hormone. Tirzepatide acts like it too, and also like a second gut hormone called GIP. Both are designed to reduce appetite and how much you eat.

visual.stock_query: two labelled hormone keys fitting locks

scenes.retention_device: Simple contrast between the two drugs

scenes.narration: Both drug labels also say these medicines delay gastric emptying. In plain English, food leaves your stomach more slowly. That's one reason a normal plate can suddenly feel like too much.

visual.stock_query: stomach character with slow conveyor belt

scenes.narration: But here's the catch. The advisory warns that eating much less can leave gaps in protein, fiber, vitamins, and minerals. Less room on the plate means every bite counts more.

visual.stock_query: small plate with gaps between nutrient icons

scenes.narration: So which gap comes first? The advisory puts one nutrient high on its list, and it's the one people ask about most.

visual.stock_query: curious woman leaning toward question mark

scenes.section: How much protein do you need?
scenes.narration: Protein. In the big weight-loss trials, part of the weight people lost was lean mass, which includes muscle. Some lean mass loss happens with weight loss in general, but it's worth protecting.

visual.stock_query: friendly muscle character holding a shield

scenes.section: How much protein do you need?
scenes.narration: That's why the advisory recommends getting enough protein, together with regular strength training. Think of protein as the bricks, and exercise as the builder who puts them to use.

visual.stock_query: cartoon builder stacking protein bricks

scenes.section: How much protein do you need?
scenes.narration: How much is right for you depends on your size, age, activity, and health. A clinician or registered dietitian can turn the advisory's recommendations into a target that fits you.

visual.stock_query: dietitian and patient planning together happily

scenes.section: How much protein do you need?
scenes.narration: One important exception. If you have kidney disease, or you've been told to limit protein, check with your clinician first before eating more of it.

visual.stock_query: kidney character holding caution sign

scenes.section: How much protein do you need?
scenes.narration: The advisory favors nutrient-dense, minimally processed foods. For protein, think fish, eggs, yogurt, beans, lentils, tofu, chicken, and nuts.

visual.stock_query: colorful protein foods smiling on shelf

scenes.section: How much protein do you need?
scenes.narration: When solid food feels like a chore, softer options can be easier: yogurt, cottage cheese, a bean soup, or a smoothie made with milk or soy milk.

visual.stock_query: cozy bowl of bean soup and smoothie

scenes.section: How much protein do you need?
scenes.narration: For Sam, that means breakfast isn't plain toast anymore. It's toast with an egg, or yogurt with berries. Same small appetite, more of what the body needs.

visual.stock_query: Sam smiling over toast with egg

scenes.section: How much protein do you need?
scenes.narration: Protein is the easy part. The harder part is what happens in your stomach in the first weeks, and the advisory has a surprisingly practical list for it.

visual.stock_query: stomach character looking nervous

scenes.narration: Let's talk about the side effects people rarely post about. The tirzepatide labels list nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, and constipation among the most common.

visual.stock_query: queasy person on couch with tea

scenes.narration: In the main tirzepatide weight trial, SURMOUNT one, nausea was reported by 31 percent of people on the top trial dose, versus 9.5 percent on placebo, over 72 weeks.

visual.stat_label: Nausea, top tirzepatide dose vs placebo, 72 weeks
visual.stock_query: stat card with calm stomach mascot

scenes.narration: That trial enrolled adults with obesity, or with overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes. The counts cover everyone who got treatment: about 630 people on the top dose and 643 on placebo.

visual.stock_query: two groups of trial volunteers labelled

scenes.narration: The researchers reported that the gastrointestinal side effects were mostly mild to moderate, and happened mainly while the dose was being stepped up.

visual.stock_query: storm cloud shrinking to small cloud

scenes.narration: So if you've felt queasy and wondered whether you're doing something wrong, you're not alone. It's common, and there are recommended ways to make meals easier.

visual.stock_query: Medi comforting worried person at kitchen table

scenes.narration: The advisory's tips include regular, smaller meals and avoiding large ones. Many people also find it helps to eat slowly and stop when they feel full, rather than when the plate is empty.

visual.stock_query: person eating slowly with small plate

scenes.narration: For queasy days, the advisory suggests going easy on fatty foods and large meals. And more generally, it recommends cutting back on sugary drinks and sweets.
scenes.on_screen_text: Go easy on fatty and sugary

visual.stock_query: fatty takeaway and soda stepping off plate

scenes.narration: For Sam, lunch might be half a chicken sandwich with salad, eaten slowly, with the other half saved for later. No rules broken, no food wasted.

visual.stock_query: Sam wrapping half sandwich, relieved

scenes.narration: One clear line, though. If vomiting or diarrhea won't settle, or you have severe stomach pain that won't go away, contact your clinician promptly. The labels flag these as reasons to get checked.
scenes.on_screen_text: Severe or lasting? Call your clinician

visual.stock_query: person calling clinician on phone calmly

scenes.narration: And don't change, skip, or stop your medicine on your own to manage side effects. That's a conversation for your prescriber.

visual.stock_query: friendly prescriber talking with patient

scenes.narration: Now, those side effects lead to a problem that's easy to miss, because it doesn't feel like nutrition at all. It's about water.

visual.stock_query: water glass with question mark

scenes.section: How much water should you drink?
scenes.narration: Here's the hidden link. The labels warn that vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration, which can lead to kidney problems, and they advise taking care not to lose too much fluid.

visual.stock_query: thirsty kidney character with water bottle

scenes.section: How much water should you drink?
scenes.narration: And when you eat less food, you also get less of the water that food usually provides. Smaller plates can quietly mean less fluid.

visual.stock_query: juicy fruit and soup on small plate

scenes.section: How much water should you drink?
scenes.narration: So the advisory recommends staying well hydrated. As a general guide, the NHS suggests 6 to 8 cups or glasses of fluid a day.

visual.stat_label: NHS: cups or glasses of fluid daily
visual.stock_query: row of cheerful glasses and mugs

scenes.section: How much water should you drink?
scenes.narration: The NHS says water, lower-fat milk, and lower-sugar drinks, including tea and coffee, all count. Small sips through the day may feel easier than big glasses at once.

visual.stock_query: person sipping tea at desk, relaxed

scenes.section: How much water should you drink?
scenes.narration: One exception: if you've been told to limit fluids, for example because of a heart or kidney condition, follow that advice instead.
scenes.on_screen_text: Told to limit fluids? Follow that

visual.stock_query: heart and kidney characters with note

scenes.section: How much water should you drink?
scenes.narration: A quick check from the NHS: signs of dehydration include dark yellow, strong-smelling pee, feeling dizzy, feeling tired, and a dry mouth. If it continues, call your clinician.

visual.stock_query: Medi holding checklist near water

scenes.section: How much water should you drink?
scenes.narration: Fluids help with the other common gut problem too: constipation. That's where fiber comes in, with one important twist.

visual.stock_query: oats and beans winking

scenes.section: How to ease constipation with fiber
scenes.narration: In SURMOUNT one, constipation was reported by about 12 to 17 percent of people across the three tirzepatide doses, versus about 6 percent on placebo, over 72 weeks.

visual.stat_label: Constipation, tirzepatide doses vs placebo, 72 weeks
visual.stock_query: stat card with gentle gut mascot

scenes.section: How to ease constipation with fiber
scenes.narration: Each tirzepatide group had about 630 to 636 people, and the placebo group had 643.

visual.stock_query: four labelled groups of people

scenes.section: How to ease constipation with fiber
scenes.narration: Fiber helps keep things moving. The NHS recommends 30 grams of fiber a day for adults, but says most adults only eat about 20 grams.

visual.stat_label: NHS daily fiber goal for adults
visual.stock_query: fiber foods filling a measuring jar

scenes.section: How to ease constipation with fiber
scenes.narration: Here's the twist: build fiber up gradually, and drink fluids alongside it. Going from low to high overnight can bring gas and bloating, the last thing an adjusting gut needs. And on queasy days early in treatment, the advisory suggests going lighter on fatty and very high-fiber foods until things settle.

visual.stock_query: staircase of fiber foods step by step

scenes.section: How to ease constipation with fiber
scenes.narration: Good fiber sources include oats, beans, lentils, vegetables, fruit, whole grains, nuts, and seeds.

visual.stock_query: happy pantry of fiber foods

scenes.section: How to ease constipation with fiber
scenes.narration: Beans and lentils are a quiet double win. They bring protein and fiber in the same spoonful.

visual.stock_query: lentil spoon with two medals

scenes.section: How to ease constipation with fiber
scenes.narration: If constipation lasts, don't just push through it. Ask your clinician or pharmacist what's suitable for you.

visual.stock_query: friendly pharmacist at counter

scenes.section: How to ease constipation with fiber
scenes.narration: So far: protein, fluids, fiber. But the advisory doesn't stop at food, and the reason goes back to that lean mass we talked about.

visual.stock_query: plate rolling toward dumbbell

scenes.narration: The advisory recommends pairing GLP-1 treatment with regular physical activity, including resistance training, to help preserve muscle and strength.

visual.stock_query: smiling person lifting light dumbbell

scenes.narration: The World Health Organization recommends adults get at least 150 to 300 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity, plus muscle-strengthening activities on two or more days.

visual.stat_label: WHO: weekly minutes of moderate activity
visual.stock_query: calendar with walking and lifting icons

scenes.narration: If that sounds like a lot, the WHO also says some physical activity is better than none. So start gently: standing up from a chair a few times, wall push-ups, carrying shopping bags, or a light resistance band.

visual.stock_query: person doing wall push-ups at home, proud

scenes.narration: If you have a health condition, or haven't exercised in a while, check with your clinician about what's safe for you.

visual.stock_query: clinician giving thumbs up to patient

scenes.narration: For Sam, that's ten minutes of chair stands and band rows after an evening walk, twice a week. Small, a little boring, and exactly the point.

visual.stock_query: Sam doing chair stands, small win

scenes.narration: Now the part most people miss. When you eat less, it's not just protein and fiber that can run low.

visual.stock_query: vitamin icons hiding behind plate

scenes.narration: The advisory flags that eating much less can raise the risk of low intake of some vitamins and minerals, such as iron, calcium, and vitamin D.

visual.stock_query: vitamin characters waving from shelf

scenes.narration: Its main answer is food first: a varied, nutrient-dense diet with vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, nuts, and protein foods, and fewer ultra-processed foods and sugary drinks.

visual.stock_query: colorful balanced plate glowing

scenes.narration: It also notes that a supplement, like a multivitamin, may be appropriate for some people. That's a question for your clinician, not a guess in the supplement aisle.

visual.myth: Everyone on GLP-1 needs a pile of supplements
visual.fact: Food first; a supplement may suit some people
visual.stock_query: confused shopper in supplement aisle

scenes.narration: And here's a recommendation that's easy to overlook. The advisory supports involving a registered dietitian, so consider asking for a referral.

visual.stock_query: warm dietitian welcoming patient

scenes.narration: A dietitian can turn general guidance into meals that fit your culture, your budget, your schedule, and your other health conditions.

visual.stock_query: family cooking diverse dishes together

scenes.narration: That matters if you take tirzepatide as Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes. The advisory was written for obesity treatment, so ask your diabetes team how these ideas fit your plan.

visual.stock_query: person chatting with diabetes care team

scenes.narration: The Mounjaro label notes that using it with insulin or a sulfonylurea can raise the risk of low blood sugar, so keep your team in the loop if your eating changes a lot.
scenes.on_screen_text: Keep your team in the loop

visual.stock_query: phone message to care team, calm

scenes.narration: So what does all of this look like on an actual plate? Let's build one sample day, and then I'll pay off that plate trick from the start.

visual.stock_query: empty plate waiting with sunrise

scenes.retention_device: Re-hook: reminder of main open loop

scenes.section: What a day of eating can look like
scenes.narration: This is one example, not a meal plan. It's just a picture of how the advisory's ideas can fit together, in portions that feel comfortable for you.

visual.stock_query: cartoon day planner with meals

scenes.section: What a day of eating can look like
scenes.narration: Breakfast: Greek yogurt with oats and berries. Or eggs on whole-grain toast with tomatoes.

visual.stock_query: yogurt bowl with berries, morning light

scenes.section: What a day of eating can look like
scenes.narration: Lunch: a lentil soup, or a small chicken and bean salad with olive oil. Eaten slowly, and finished when you're comfortably full.

visual.stock_query: steaming lentil soup at lunch

scenes.section: What a day of eating can look like
scenes.narration: A snack, if you want one: a handful of nuts, a glass of milk or soy milk, or hummus with carrot sticks.

visual.stock_query: hummus and carrot sticks, cheerful

scenes.section: What a day of eating can look like
scenes.narration: Dinner: fish or tofu, a small portion of brown rice or potatoes, and cooked vegetables.

visual.stock_query: salmon with rice and vegetables

scenes.section: What a day of eating can look like
scenes.narration: And fluids across the whole day: water, tea, milk, a mug of broth. Not one giant glass at bedtime.

visual.stock_query: clock with mugs around it

scenes.section: What a day of eating can look like
scenes.narration: Notice what's missing. No calorie target, no skipped meals, no special GLP-1 diet. The advisory's focus is food quality and getting enough nutrients, not eating as little as possible.

visual.myth: On GLP-1, eat as little as possible
visual.fact: Focus on food quality and enough nutrients
visual.stock_query: Medi crossing out tiny empty plate

scenes.narration: Now, the plate trick I promised. It's simple: eat the protein on your plate first.

visual.stock_query: cloche lifted revealing protein first

scenes.narration: Here's why. When fullness arrives after a few bites, whatever you ate first is what you actually got. If those first bites are bread or chips, the protein gets left behind.

visual.stock_query: chicken left alone on plate, sad

scenes.narration: So start with the fish, eggs, beans, or yogurt. Then the vegetables. Then the rest, if there's room.

visual.stock_query: plate divided into numbered sections

scenes.narration: And this isn't just our idea. The joint advisory itself suggests eating protein-rich foods first in a meal, to make it more likely you get enough. It's practical advice, not something tested as a rule in tirzepatide trials.
scenes.on_screen_text: Advisory tip, not a trial result

visual.stock_query: Medi pointing at advisory badge, honest

scenes.retention_device: Authority reveal that strengthens the payoff

scenes.narration: For Sam, that one change means the chicken gets eaten before the fries, every time. The appetite didn't get bigger. The plate just got smarter.

visual.stock_query: Sam cheering a small win at dinner

scenes.narration: Here's your checklist. One: build smaller meals around a protein food, and eat it first. Two: build fiber up gradually, with fluids.

visual.stock_query: clipboard with green checkmarks

factcheck.summary:
The script is accurate and safe, and it passes with four minor wording fixes listed below. I checked it against the sources it cites.

**Joint advisory (Obesity 2025;33(8):1475–1503).** It says everything the script attributes to it:
- Small, frequent meals and avoiding large ones.
- Enough protein, with protein-rich foods eaten first in a meal (the plate trick).
- Building fibre up gradually.
- Enough fluids.
- Cutting back on sugary drinks and sweets.
- Resistance training.
- Iron, calcium and vitamin D among the nutrients of concern, with a multivitamin as an option for some people.
- Involving a registered dietitian.
- Part of the weight lost in the trials being lean mass.

**SURMOUNT-1.** All the numbers match:
- Nausea: 31.0% on 15 mg vs 9.5% on placebo.
- Constipation: 16.8%, 17.1% and 11.7% across the three doses vs 5.8% on placebo.
- Group sizes in the safety population: 630, 636 and 630 vs 643.
- Stomach and gut side effects were mostly mild to moderate and mainly happened while the dose was being stepped up.

**NHS and WHO.** The NHS lines match: 6 to 8 cups or glasses a day, the list of drinks that count, 30 g of fibre against an average of about 20 g, and the dehydration signs. So do the WHO lines: 150 to 300 minutes a week, strength training on 2 or more days, and some activity being better than none.

**Safety.** The safety caveats are all there: kidney disease and protein, fluid limits, low blood sugar when used with insulin or a sulfonylurea, don't change your medicine on your own, contact a clinician for severe or lasting symptoms, start exercise gently, and the prescriber line. The script doesn't push restrictive eating. Sam is clearly labelled as hypothetical. The title is 60 characters and the video pays it off.

**What to fix.**
- Eating slowly and stopping when full sits under the advisory's source tag, but the advisory doesn't say it.
- Two lines widen the advisory's 'first few days of treatment' to 'queasy days'.
- Scene s73's on-screen checklist runs ahead of the narration.

**Sources.** I couldn't open the Lilly press release URL directly (it returned a 403 error), but a search confirmed it exists and has the quoted figures. The NEJM paper is paywalled. The PubMed page didn't load in my tool, so I couldn't check the abstract (S-PM) myself; the press release and the advisory back up the trial figures. I couldn't fetch the three drug labels (Z, M, W), but what the script attributes to them matches the standard US prescribing information.

issues.claim: The advisory's tips include regular, smaller meals and avoiding large ones. Many people also find it helps to eat slowly and stop when they feel full, rather than when the plate is empty.
issues.problem: The scene is tagged to source A, but the advisory doesn't mention eating slowly or stopping when full. 'Many people also find' is also an unsourced claim about experience. Our own tips shouldn't sit under a source tag or be dressed up as evidence.
issues.fix: Narration: "The advisory's tips include regular, smaller meals and avoiding large ones. A simple habit that can help too: eat slowly, and stop when you feel full, rather than when the plate is empty." Leave source_ids as ["A"] for the first sentence only. In s75, keep the source tag on 'small and regular' and 'fatty foods and sugary drinks' only.

issues.claim: And on queasy days early in treatment, the advisory suggests going lighter on fatty and very high-fiber foods until things settle.
issues.problem: This widens the advisory's scope. It says 'avoiding fatty or high fiber foods during the first few days of treatment can help alleviate symptoms', not 'on queasy days … until things settle'.

audio.soundNotes: Music sits well in the -12/-15 window already (−13.5 under voice) but the pause level is a touch loud at −13.2 vs the −14 target, so I trimmed the whole bed ~0.6 dB with the 0.93 multiplier — keeps it felt-not-competing in pauses without starving it under speech. The big fix is a dozen-plus stock SFX that leaked to −4 to −12 dB relative to the voice while the narrator was still talking (chips reveal at 130.4s, the pop/whoosh at 387.8s, the fluids/apnea/pharmacist/closing beats) — pulled those down 6–13 dB so they're felt, not heard over words, matching the rest of the kit that was already sitting correctly near −14 to −18 dB. Also thinned three overcrowded SFX clusters (chips callouts around 360s, 428s and 447s had 5–7 hits in under 1.5s) down to 3–4 events each. Added five bespoke cues for key story beats: a warm welcome chime for 'Meet Sam', a counter-reveal ding under the SURMOUNT-1 stat, a tonal pivot swell at 'Now, the harder part', a slow deep heartbeat under the dehydration/kidney warning, and a calm reassurance chime on the 'Not personal advice' card — each kept low (0.15–0.22 gain) so they color the moment without ever crowding the narration.

thumbnail.reasoning: All three are legible, on-brand, single-focal-point designs with no misleading claims. #0 ('4 BITES') has the strongest hook: it names the exact relatable moment (appetite crashes to almost nothing on tirzepatide) that the title's 'When Appetite Drops' promises to solve, paired with a single surprised plate character and minimal, large, 2-line text that reads instantly even at 168px. #1 ('EAT THIS FIRST') is a close second with a good before/after contrast concept, but it packs in two characters, a VS, and two small pill labels (BIG MEAL / PROTEIN PLATE) that add clutter and shrink at phone size, slightly hurting instant legibility. #2 ('PROTEIN FIRST?') is clean and legible but its fish mascot doesn't visually connect to 'protein' or eating, weakening the curiosity payoff and emotional pull compared to the other two. #0 wins on CTR while keeping legibility ≥7.
